item.title: Wildfire Smoke Chokes Skies in Spain and France
item.description:
Wildfires in France and Spain this past week have blazed toward cities, forced evacuations by land and sea and wreathed the skies of southern Europe in stifling smoke.

Already broiling under intense summer heat, some 200,000 people in France and Spain have fled their homes or were ordered to remain indoors as dozens of fires moved across parts of each country. In France, one official called two severe fires the “ogres of the summer.” In Spain, another labeled one blaze “the worst wildfire in the Madrid region’s history.”

The Spanish government has declared the fires in the Madrid region a national emergency, and both countries have requested additional aid from the European Union to combat the fires and help people affected.

Firefighters battled flames on Friday in a forest in Lège-Cap-Ferret, in southwestern France.

A French Civil Security aircraft flying past flames on Thursday in a forest surrounding Cotignac, in southeastern France.

Students from a martial arts gym worked to extinguish a fire outside their teacher’s home on Friday in the village of El Tiemblo, Spain.

People who left Lège-Cap-Ferret arrived in Arcachon, across the Arcachon Bay, during an evacuation of the Cap Ferret peninsula in France on Friday.

Evacuees sheltered from wildfires on Friday in Cebreros, Spain, west of Madrid.

Traffic jams built up from the areas threatened by the fire. Cap Ferret, a popular vacation destination, is a geographically isolated peninsula with one major road going in and out.

Smoke darkened the skies near the beach on Thursday in Andernos-les-Bains, in southwestern France.

Juana Gonzalez, a resident of El Tiemblo, Spain, covered her face to protect herself from smoke on Friday.

Firefighters in Spain carried out controlled burns in the village of Navas del Rey to slow the spread of wildfires.

A firefighter working near a burning building on Thursday in Lège-Cap-Ferret, France.

Some evacuees in Spain took shelter from the wildfires in a Madrid sports center.

A wildfire burned in a forest near the Arcachon Bay on Friday.

item.title: What to Know About the Wildfires Raging in Western Europe
item.description:
Fast-moving wildfires fueled by extreme heat and strong winds have forced some 200,000 people to flee or remain indoors this past week in France and Spain as firefighters struggle to bring the blazes under control.

No deaths have been linked to the fires, which have mainly hit southwestern France, near Bordeaux, and central Spain, near Madrid.

But the flames have torn through tens of thousands of acres of land, injured dozens of firefighters, destroyed scores of homes and campsites and forced many vacationers to flee popular summertime spots.

The Spanish and French authorities have requested additional resources from the European Union and warned that high temperatures and erratic gusts were making it difficult to stop the flames.

The authorities have reported dozens of wildfires in France, but the biggest and most worrying blazes are near the Atlantic coastline, in the southwestern region that includes Bordeaux.

One started on Wednesday in the Gironde area, while the other started on Thursday in the Landes area, farther south, according to local authorities. Those fires have burned over 120,000 acres so far.

The French authorities have also expressed concern about fires in the country’s southeastern Var area that have burned over 8,000 acres.

The fire in the Gironde area “generates its own winds, accelerates its spread and can abruptly change direction,” Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu of France said late Friday.

“Civil protection experts had never before encountered such a phenomenon,” Mr. Lecornu said on social media after a government crisis meeting.

In Spain, wildfires in the mountains west of Madrid forced more than 19,000 people to evacuate and burned almost 15,000 acres by Friday afternoon. The blazes were closing in on populated areas.

“This is the worst wildfire in the Madrid region’s history,” Isabel Díaz Ayuso, the regional president, said on Friday. The fires spread amid “a perfect storm of extremely high temperatures and relentless winds,” she added, although the authorities in the Madrid region said on social media on Saturday that conditions had improved, with less wind, higher humidity and lower temperatures.

The Spanish and French authorities have ordered thousands to evacuate, set up emergency shelters, deployed firefighting planes and helicopters and sent security and military reinforcements to bolster hundreds of firefighters who are battling flames around the clock.

On Saturday, the prefect for the Gironde area ordered the evacuation of several western suburbs of Bordeaux as a precautionary measure. One includes the city’s airport. Thousands of people had previously evacuated the Cap Ferret peninsula, a popular Atlantic holiday destination. Hundreds fled by boat.

President Emmanuel Macron of France has asked the country’s armed forces “to mobilize to provide maximum support to civil security,” his office said on Friday evening. Over 1,000 soldiers are expected on the ground on Saturday, according to Mr. Lecornu, the prime minister.

The French authorities also announced on Friday that they were sending 1.5 million face masks to protect residents and emergency workers from toxic smoke caused by the fires.

The exact origins of the blazes in France and Spain were not immediately clear, but they are part of a broader surge of wildfires this summer across Europe fueled by repeated heat waves since late May.

The heat waves have parched vegetation and melted glaciers and have been linked to thousands of excess deaths. Last month was the hottest June on record in Western Europe, according to Copernicus, a European Union monitoring agency.

Connecting a specific heat wave or fire to global warming is hard to do, but experts agree that human-caused climate change is behind the increasingly high temperatures that have made wildfires more destructive in general.

About two weeks ago, a wildfire in the southeastern Spanish province of Almería killed 13 people, making it one of the country’s deadliest fires on record. Two French firefighters died battling a previous fire near Bordeaux this week.

France has decades of experience with wildfires in the country’s south, but the blazes have increased in number and pushed north as summer temperatures rise. By mid-July, almost 11,000 fires had already started across the country and burned more acres than throughout the entirety of last summer.

Carlos Barragán contributed reporting from Madrid.

item.title: Forced to Flee and Wait, Evacuees Wonder if Their Homes Still Stand
item.description:
Arantxa Alcázar stepped into her garden on Thursday when she heard police officers shouting at residents to evacuate their homes in Villa del Prado, a town west of Madrid. The blazes that had been raging in the distant mountains were now sweeping down their street.

“Like a river of fire,” she said.

She fled with her mother, Consuelo Lorza, 88, and her 11-year-old daughter, Sara, to another town, only to have to evacuate again hours later, to a nearby village. The following day, they were forced to flee once more, this time to the town of Villamanta.

“I’ve been sleeping here for three days — if you can call that sleep,” Ms. Lorza said on Sunday morning. She shared a bunk with her granddaughter, while Ms. Alcázar spent the night in her car with the family dog. They eventually found out that Ms. Alcázar’s home had been spared.

More than 200 people were staying on makeshift bunks inside a sports hall in Villamanta on Sunday, anxiously waiting to learn whether they would be allowed to return home or whether the flames were advancing toward them. Some tried to nap after lunch while children kicked a football around, using one of the hall’s goals.

In total, around 90,000 people in central Spain had been evacuated from their homes or ordered to take shelter as firefighters battled what Isabel Díaz Ayuso, the Madrid region’s president, described as “the worst wildfire” in the region’s history.

Ms. Lorza had just been comforted by King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, who visited the sports hall to show their support. “The queen told me she couldn’t believe it. Evacuated three times!” Ms. Lorza said.

King Felipe VI said on Sunday that the wildfires in Madrid and the neighboring Toledo and Ávila regions remained active but that there were some “positive signs” in the fight against the blazes.

In the Madrid region, fire had destroyed 43 homes and severely damaged more than 300 others, Ms. Díaz Ayuso said. “That number will rise enormously, as we have never seen before,” she said, tears welling in her eyes.

Across central Spain, 77,000 hectares — about 190,000 acres — have burned, the country’s public broadcaster reported.

Some evacuees in Villamanta complained that they had received little information about the status of the fires. They waited nervously near their cars, eating churros.

“We watch the fires every minute” through security camera feeds, said Carmen Bautista, 53, who had slept, along with her husband, in their van beside the sports center. They had watched the flames approach their home in Caravan Garden, a nearby development, but it was now safe.

Ms. Bautista lamented that residents had endured one natural disaster after another — the pandemic, then the deadly floods that swept away three bridges — and that each one seemed worse than the last.

“With the previous catastrophes, you could stay at home. Now …” she broke off, spreading her arms in resignation.

While firefighters struggled to bring the blazes under control, some residents took matters into their own hands. In the mountains around Robledo de Chavela, where the flames had torn through pine forests and holm oaks, several residents on Saturday slipped past police roadblocks to fight the fires.

“We may be doing something slightly illegal, but we have saved this part of the mountain,” Javier Quijada, 30, said on a video call. Mr. Quijada and dozens of other residents, all members of the local hunting association, had been fighting the flames with hoses, shovels and even green branches they used to try to smother the fire. He said police officers eventually waved them through, warning them to be careful.

“This is our mountain. Our lives are going up in flames,” Mr. Quijada said. “I’ve lost count of how many tears I’ve shed since the fire began.”

item.title: A South African Identity Crisis
item.description:
Katrin is away this week, so I’ll be hosting the newsletter. Today’s is about the increasingly scary climate for immigrants in South Africa.

A few months ago, amid concerns about anti-immigrant violence, Ghana chartered a flight to repatriate 300 of its citizens from South Africa. It was an “extraordinary move,” John Eligon, our Johannesburg bureau chief, wrote at the time — but other countries soon followed suit. In the weeks since, Kenya, Malawi, Nigeria and Uganda have also organized repatriation efforts.

This isn’t the first time that South Africa has been rocked by xenophobic violence. But it seems different this time around. The anti-immigrant activists are more organized; the pushback from other African countries has been fiercer. Today, John writes about how the latest protests have led to an identity crisis in South Africa.

By John Eligon

As part of my reporting on anti-immigrant activists, I recently tagged along with a group of South Africans who were going to raid a house that they believed had been illegally occupied by undocumented foreigners.

When we got there, the activists forced their way through burglar bars and banged the front door open. What I saw next was terrifying and sad: a line of shivering young children shuffling out, choking back tears. Their mother, Sandra, a 38-year-old asylum seeker from the Democratic Republic of Congo, emerged with fear in her eyes. She had no idea who these people were or what they had come to do.

But the activists showed little sympathy. “You can go back to your country,” a member of the mob yelled. They dumped the family’s belongings on the sidewalk, and then refused to let the mother and children back in the house.

Such is life these days in South Africa, which has recently been convulsed by a spasm of anti-immigrant threats, violence and protests.

The country is no stranger to this kind of xenophobic outrage, which has popped up every few years since 2008. This time, though, things feel a little different.

Anti-immigrant activists appear to have become more organized than in years past. Much of the unrest has been fueled by groups that coordinate nationwide marches and push campaigns on social media. The activists set an artificial deadline of June 30 for all undocumented foreigners to leave South Africa — a threat that prompted many migrants to flee and that set off panic across the country.

This all amplifies what seems to be an identity crisis in South Africa. It is a nation that holds tremendous wealth but also struggles with inequality and a high unemployment rate, which hovers at around 30 percent. South Africa projects itself as a bastion of human rights, but today it’s confronting gruesome episodes of vigilante violence.

Violence and intimidation

Coverage of African migration tends to focus on those who try to reach Europe on rickety boats, but most people stay within Africa. Many end up heading to South Africa because it has the largest economy in the continent.

But here you hear the same nativist arguments as in other parts of the world: They’re taking our jobs. They’re committing crimes. They’re straining our resources.

Officially, about three million immigrants live in South Africa, or about 5 percent of the population. There are a lot more who are undocumented.

I’ve talked to many immigrants in recent weeks who shared how citizens had barged into their homes and businesses, telling them to leave and to shut down their shops. One clip making the rounds on social media shows Emeka Nwankpu, who is from Nigeria, being confronted by anti-immigrant activists outside the shop he owns. He explained that he was in the country legally, had a business permit and employed tens of South Africans.

The activists didn’t care. “We don’t want any foreigners to run any business here, including you,” one of the them tells him in the video, jabbing a finger in his face. “So today you’re closing.”

This kind of hostility has prompted many migrants to set up makeshift camps outside consulates and embassies in South Africa’s major cities, where they await help to leave the country. It’s startling to see thousands of people sitting on bags and suitcases — tired, scared and disheveled — on the streets.

An identity crisis

The current moment reveals the contradictions that live in the minds of many South Africans.

The same South Africans who celebrate their country’s exceptionalism because of its economy and development are also quick to say that the economy can’t handle an influx of migrants. And the same government officials who warn citizens not to turn to vigilantism also blame migrants for many of the country’s challenges.

So now the country that was once seen as a global human rights darling, heralded for the leadership of Nelson Mandela and for defeating the blatant institutionalized racism of apartheid, is struggling to defend its reputation. South Africa has faced more international pressure than it did during previous xenophobic flare-ups. Officials from African countries have been particularly critical, saying that their citizens are bearing the brunt of the violence and the threats.

The country breathed a collective sigh of relief when June 30 came and went without any major violence or destruction.

But one of the anti-immigrant activists I have been following had a bitter taste in her mouth the next day. While immigrant-owned businesses were mostly closed on June 30 for safety, they were back open again the next day. She resolved to continue fighting until all the migrants were gone, once and for all.

Read John’s story about one mother’s crusade to rid South Africa of African immigrants.

item.title: What to Know About the Fatal Attack Near a Pride Celebration
item.description:
A car plowed through a park during Berlin’s biggest L.G.B.T.Q. Pride event late Saturday local time, killing at least one person and injuring 29 others, the authorities said. After an intense 18-hour manhunt, the man whom police called the prime suspect died in a police raid after he charged at officers with a weapon.

Here’s what to know.

The violence occurred in the Tiergarten, a large central park in Berlin where large crowds had gathered to celebrate the annual L.G.B.T.Q. Pride festival, also known as Christopher Street Day, that is among the biggest such events in Europe.

Hundreds of thousands of people were in Berlin celebrating the festival, and many had gathered in the park, dancing to music and watching the parade. Around 10 p.m., a white minivan sped down a side street leading out of the park. The vehicle was eventually found abandoned where it had crashed into a tree. Officials said Sunday the attacker had also wielded what appeared to be a machete.

One woman was killed and 29 others were injured, many of them critically, the police said. Some victims suffered stab wounds, the police added.

The police identified the suspect only as Abdul B., in keeping with German privacy laws, and said that he was already known to law enforcement and active in local Islamist groups.

The man, a 21-year-old German citizen whose family members migrated from Lebanon, had been the subject of a protracted nationwide manhunt since the Saturday evening attack. The suspect used a rented van and what appeared to be a machete in the attack, which German officials called an act of Islamist terrorism.

In a brief statement, the police said they had tracked the suspect to an area in a western corner of the city where residents maintain large garden patches. After officers shot him, emergency responders tried to revive him, but he died at the scene, the police said.

The authorities said their investigation into the attack was continuing.

The attack put an abrupt end to Christopher Street Day, a raucous festival that earlier Saturday had been the scene of dancing, celebrations and music. Officials canceled the rest of the program, which had been scheduled to continue on Sunday.

“This is an attack on our society,” Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, wrote on the social media platform X. “The crime will be investigated and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law,” he added.

Kai Wegner, Berlin’s mayor, said in a news release that “after a peaceful and vibrant Christopher Street Day, the gathering for a tolerant and peaceful Berlin was brutally attacked. Berlin is the city of freedom — and our freedom has been horribly attacked today.”

Almost immediately, the attack reignited a debate in Germany about migration, religious extremism and public safety. It came months before Berlin and two other eastern states are set to hold closely watched regional elections, where polls already have suggested far-right parties are poised to make gains, partly on the basis of Germans’ anxieties over public violence.

item.title: Berlin Police Search for Suspect in Fatal Attack on Pride Parade
item.description:
An overnight manhunt for the attacker who killed a woman and injured several others at a Berlin gay Pride celebration stretched into midday Sunday with no resolution in sight, as the authorities asked the public to help find a young man they said had ties to Islamic extremist groups.

Berlin police said they were searching for “at least one suspect” after the attack on the annual Christopher Street Day parade, which drew hundreds of thousands of revelers to Berlin’s city center on Saturday. The festivities included a concert on Saturday evening near the Brandenburg Gate and the Tiergarten, the city’s large central park.

Shortly after 10 p.m., the authorities said, a white minivan sped through a side street leading out of the park, eventually crashing into a tree. The driver ran away. Video footage showed the car’s front grill smashed and its body heavily dented.

At least 16 people were left injured, some critically, after the attack. The police said some had suffered stab wounds. Local officials said they would release more information at a news conference Sunday afternoon.

Early Sunday morning, the police released a photograph and a partial name of a suspected attacker, in an appeal for public help in locating the man, Abdul B., 21. His full surname was withheld under German privacy laws.

The police said he was known to them and was associated with what they called “the Islamist spectrum.” They said they were investigating the attack as an act of terrorism.

Several German media outlets reported that the suspect was born in Germany and held a German passport, and that he had a migration background from Lebanon.

The police would not immediately confirm those reports. Nor did they say if the man had links to any foreign actors.

In recent months, as the United States and Israel have engaged in war against Iran, German intelligence officials have privately warned of the threat of Tehran-sponsored attacks on German soil.

Police and media reports suggested the search for the suspect had sprawled across Berlin and out to Germany’s borders, with the authorities running down multiple leads. Several outlets reported that officers searched an apartment in a neighborhood less than a mile from the Tiergarten, where the suspect was said to live with his mother, but that they did not find him there.

The attack abruptly ended a celebration that drew hundreds of thousands of revelers to Berlin, with organizers canceling a final slate of planned events on Sunday morning.

It rattled a community that had spent much of the day dancing in colorful costumes under idyllic summer skies.

It also immediately reignited a debate in Germany about migration, religious extremism and public safety. It came months before Berlin and two other eastern states are set to hold closely watched regional elections, where polls already have suggested far-right parties are poised to make gains, partly on the basis of Germans’ anxieties over public violence.

“This is an attack on our society,” Chancellor Friedrich Merz of Germany wrote on X early Sunday morning. “The crime will be investigated and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law,” he added.

Kai Wegner, Berlin’s mayor, said in a news release that “after a peaceful and vibrant Christopher Street Day, the gathering for a tolerant and peaceful Berlin was brutally attacked. Berlin is the city of freedom — and our freedom has been horribly attacked today.”

The event, named for the New York City street known for its association with the Stonewall riots that sparked the modern gay rights movement, draws hundreds of thousands of people to Berlin each year.

Early Sunday, roads near the site of the suspected attack were blocked off by a heavy police presence. Nearby, emergency personnel had erected a tent to take care of distraught witnesses. Some were seen hugging each other, and some had thermal blankets wrapped around them.

Hours earlier, barricades had blocked vehicle traffic on roads leading through the Tiergarten, while throngs of revelers, many wearing glittery, colorful outfits, danced to the throbbing sounds of techno music, spilling into cafes and beer gardens nearby. The barricades were, in many places, large and fence-like, and it was unclear how a car could have driven past or through them.

By late evening, the sounds of celebration had given way to the blare of sirens and the drone of helicopters circling over the area.

Pranav Baskar contributed reporting. Verena Hölzl contributed from Berlin.

item.title: The Accidental Hero Who Faced Down India’s Government
item.description:
Abhijeet Dipke peered at the phone screen to see with his own eyes if what he’d just heard was true. For more than two months, Mr. Dipke had led a protest movement demanding the resignation of India’s education minister — and now, he had gotten his wish.

Mr. Dipke fell to his knees and repeatedly punched the makeshift stage at New Delhi’s main protest site in excitement. Then he rose up, grabbed a microphone and delivered the news to the sea of protesters around him.

“Long live student power,” Mr. Dipke shouted, pumping his fist repeatedly. “We have done it!”

The crowd erupted into deafening applause, cheering, pumping their fists into the air and sharing group hugs. Mr. Dipke, 30, who had already built a gigantic following after founding a movement through which India’s youth could channel their frustrations, had cemented his status as a folk hero.

He had taken on the government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and scored a victory.

Barely two months before, Mr. Dipke was just another “international student from India,” with a master’s degree in public relations from Boston University, squeezing in workouts in between applying for jobs and playing FIFA soccer on his PlayStation, he said in an interview on Saturday from his perch onstage.

Hours before he heard that the government had acquiesced to the students’ demands, he described his journey from introverted student to leader of a mass movement.

On May 16, Mr. Dipke woke up in Boston to a comment made by the Chief Justice of India, Surya Kant, comparing unemployed Indian youth to “parasites” and “cockroaches.”

Mr. Dipke said that he had been taken aback that the country’s top judge would refer to India’s youth in such a disparaging manner.

“I felt really hurt and humiliated,” he recalled.

And so he posted a simple question on the social media platform X: “What if all cockroaches came together?”

Mr. Dipke said that he hadn’t expected his musing to hold much power until he saw that millions of people — while embracing the humor — had also taken his post as a call to action. Within two days, he had built a website using A.I. tools, roping in some friends to help. Thus, the Cockroach Janta Party was born, the name a parody of the Bharatiya Janata Party of India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi. Membership was open to the “lazy,” the “unemployed” and anyone who “just rants.” Within two weeks, the Cockroach party’s Instagram account had picked up 22 million followers.

Mr. Dipke’s timing was impeccable. Barely two weeks earlier, India’s medical-college entrance exam, which 2.2 million aspiring doctors and dentists had taken, was canceled after the discovery that some questions had leaked beforehand. Such leaks are almost endemic to India’s education system and regularly prompt fury and frustration.

To bring lasting change, though, Mr. Dipke and others spearheading the Cockroach movement would have to figure out how to alchemize the energy of the nascent movement.

Although India has a long history of democratic demonstrations, the space for any kind of agitation has eroded under the Modi administration. Mr. Dipke said that he decided to return to India in early June to start a protest, despite fearing that he might be jailed or attacked.

“I’m not a national security threat,” he said. “I’m a citizen of this country who loves this country.”

Less than two weeks after Mr. Dipke’s initial post, his Cockroach movement started protests in New Delhi in early June, next to an 18th-century observatory called Jantar Mantar.

“How long will we live in fear of this government?” he asked the hundreds of people who first gathered there.

For weeks, demonstrators camped out. Mr. Dipke and his team repeatedly urged protesters to keep their rallies peaceful as security forces maintained a heavy presence. Many protesters carried images of Gandhi and B.R. Ambedkar, another central figure in India’s independence movement who embraced nonviolent protest.

“Our movement is peaceful,” Mr. Dipke said on Saturday, blaming the authorities for clashes with security officers as protesters tried to march to Parliament on Monday. The police said in a statement that demonstrators that day had become “unruly, aggressive, and violent.”

Mr. Dipke started his protest with a core demand: India’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, must resign because the exam leak had happened under his watch.

Mr. Modi’s government largely ignored the demonstrations, even as they spread. Students made up the bulk of the protesters, but they were joined by people of all ages demanding accountability. Sonam Wangchuk, a prominent education activist, went on a hunger strike for 26 days in support of the movement.

The government first showed signs of listening as public outrage grew over the beating of protesters. They proposed talks at a senior minister’s residence. Mr. Dipke and his colleagues pushed back, insisting that government officials either came to Jantar Mantar or met with them at a neutral venue. They rejected some government proposals, such as a law against leaking exam papers, as inadequate.

Eventually, three rounds of talks were held at a neutral venue over five days between a Cockroach party delegation and two senior ministers, Jagat Prakash Nadda and Jitendra Singh.

Then came the phone call to Mr. Dipke late Saturday afternoon as he stood onstage. The government had agreed to nearly everything the party had demanded. It vowed to pay compensation to the families of students who died by suicide after the exam leak. It agreed to withdraw police cases against protesters. And it promised to discuss a five-point charter on broader exam and education overhauls.

After the agreement, Mr. Dipke’s colleagues announced that their protests was being called off “in good faith,” shaking hands with government officials in a scene that weeks earlier would have seemed unthinkable.

Although Mr. Dipke has an enormous following — every day, people stood in line for hours waiting to shake his hand — he said that he wasn’t sure whether he saw himself as a political leader. Calling himself a “big introvert” who enjoys history books and documentaries, he said he wanted to keep the limelight on the movement rather than on himself.

He added that he also worried about his parents, who live in the state of Maharashtra, in central India. His mother, who breaks down on every phone call, he said, “kind of weakens me as well.” Since returning to India, Mr. Dipke has spent only two days at his family home. He is also recovering from a bout of typhoid, he said, and therefore avoids video calls with his parents so as not to alarm them about his health.

By midmorning on Sunday, the street outside Jantar Mantar was quiet. Rows of yellow police barricades were stacked along the roadside. Workers picked up trash and painted over the graffiti that protesters had left on the brick walls.

Vijay Solanki, who recently completed an engineering degree, said that he admired Mr. Dipke for making people believe in the power of action. “Most of us were frustrated, but we didn’t know where to put that frustration,” Mr. Solanki, 26, said. “He brought students together for the first time, it felt like our voices were actually being heard.”

item.title: Flames Advance on Bordeaux, Where Evacuees Balance Dread and Hope
item.description:
As a fierce, fast-moving, and capricious wildfire spread to within 10 miles of Bordeaux on Sunday, the city, France’s sixth largest, had become a refuge for thousands of people evacuated from their towns and villages.

Many of them took shelter in Bordeaux’s cavernous exhibition center, united by fear, confusion, and a determination to get back their homes, which they desperately hoped would be spared by the flames.

There are differing voices in this instant community, attesting to the divergent lives of the people across the Gironde region. Fear is leavened by hope, gratitude to the firefighters is tinged by anger toward the authorities, and optimism in a swift recovery is offset by uneasiness about the natural forces that led to this disaster.

“I don’t want to start again at zero to find a new apartment,” said Imane El Idrissi, 35, a single mother who fled at 4 a.m. on Saturday, after the police pounded on her door to warn her it was time to leave. “I don’t have the means.”

Ms. El Idrissi, who was born in Morocco, said she had carefully gathered all her immigration and residency documents, filling her suitcase with papers in place of clothing. Her two daughters were born in France, she said, but she couldn’t shake the fear that if she left the country, she might not be allowed back in.

Her friend, Atika Farhati, 77, a retired hospital worker, said she worried about losing her apartment and treasured possessions, including a Chinese vase. Her town, Eysines, northwest of Bordeaux, lies in the path of the fires, which were blown east by swirling winds from the Atlantic toward the city.

“The sky was red,” she said, recalling the flame-scarred view from her fifth-floor balcony. “Now that we’re here, we can only wonder how it’s going to end.”

For Roger Peuron, that outcome is not seriously in doubt. A retired engineer who worked at an armaments factory in Saint-Médard-en-Jalles, Mr. Peuron, 89, said he was confident the fire would be stopped short of his town, if only to prevent it from igniting a factory that makes fuel for strategic ballistic missiles.

“If that ever happened to the industry,” he said, “it would be a true catastrophe.”

Still, Mr. Peuron said France had never witnessed a fire like this, and it raised profound questions about how people should change their relationship to their environment. Sprawling pine forests that were planted across the region over centuries are now an accelerant for fire.

“We need to replace the trees because the sap in the pines is flammable, and the trees don’t have deep roots, so they are easily blown over by the wind,” Mr. Peuron said. “The pines were planted to drain the region’s swamps, but they’re no longer suited to the environment.”

“We need sequoias,” he added. “They’re sturdy!”

French officials backed up Mr. Peuron’s contention about the extraordinary nature of the fire, reflecting a warming climate. About 42,000 hectares, or 103,000 acres, have burned in Gironde since the fire started last week. It has forced the evacuation of about 220,000 people, one of the largest peacetime evacuations in French history.

At the same time, fires in central Spain have burned about 50,000 hectares and displaced 105,000 people.

So far this summer, forest fires have burned 115,000 hectares in France, according to the French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez. By comparison, the average yearly loss from 2014 to 2023 was 9,000 hectares. In the summer of 2022, which was considered devastating and led France to bolster its firefighting resources, about 70,000 hectares burned.

On Sunday, a heavy yellow-orange cloud of smoke hung over Bordeaux, an elegant city of 260,000 that is famous as the center of France’s wine industry. An acrid smell pervaded its streets, and tiny particles of soot flecked the air. Pedestrians wore face masks, and many shut themselves in their homes.

As the fire crept toward the city limits, Bordeaux’s mayor, Thomas Cazenave, said on Sunday that the authorities did not expect they would have to order an evacuation. But he and other officials warned that uncertainty was the watchword, as shifting winds and heat made it difficult for firefighters to gain control of the blaze.

The forecast for Bordeaux calls for high temperatures of 37 degrees Celsius on Tuesday and 41 on Wednesday — about 99 and 106 degrees Fahrenheit.

At the exhibition center, the talk was of how long people would have to wait before they would be allowed back home. People passed the time reading, playing cards, and, in the case of one young man, Julien Hochard, picking at his guitar.

“There’s a solidarity that we’ve seen emerge here, one that’s slowly growing,” said Mr. Hochard, sitting on a camp bed next to his friend, Céline Lartigue. She said she had been impressed by firefighters’ efforts to stem the blaze.

But from a nearby bed, Rabah Boukabous piped up to disagree.

“I think the authorities reacted late,” he said. “They should have recognized the gravity of the situation.”

“They could not have prevented it,” said Mr. Boukabous, 70, “but they could have limited it.”

Catherine Porter contributed reporting from Paris
